title: Antimicrobial Resistance at Slaughterhouse and Meat-Processing Interfaces in East Africa: A One Health Review of Contamination Pathways, Occupational Exposure and Control Strategies
content: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major One Health challenge because resistant microorganisms and resistance determinants can circulate among humans, animals and the environment. Slaughterhouses and meat-processing facilities represent important interfaces within this interconnected system. Animals carrying resistant bacteria may introduce them into slaughter environments, where contamination can occur through gastrointestinal contents, hides, carcasses, workers’ hands, knives, equipment, water and processing surfaces. These pathways may expose workers and consumers while contributing to the wider environmental dissemination of resistant microorganisms. This review examines evidence concerning AMR at slaughterhouse and meat-processing interfaces in East Africa, with emphasis on contamination pathways, occupational exposure, bacterial resistance patterns, genomic evidence and feasible control strategies. A targeted narrative literature search was conducted using PubMed-indexed records, PubMed Central, publisher platforms, institutional repositories and international policy sources. Relevant evidence was identified from Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda and Ethiopia. Studies from western Kenya have demonstrated resistant bacteria in slaughterhouse environments, carcasses and workers, while investigations in Tanzania have identified antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli in goat meat and meat-handler-associated isolates. Evidence from Ethiopia has documented Salmonella and Staphylococcus aureus contamination across carcasses, workers and processing environments. A 2026 investigation in southwestern Uganda additionally reported antimicrobial residues and resistant bacteria in beef samples. Genomic investigations from Tanzania have identified extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing E. coli, including isolates carrying blaCTX-M-15 and multidrug-resistance-associated plasmids. However, the available evidence is geographically uneven, methodologically heterogeneous and insufficient to establish the direction or frequency of transmission between animals, workers, meat and environmental compartments. Important limitations include inconsistent sampling designs, variable antimicrobial susceptibility testing, limited genomic surveillance and a lack of longitudinal studies linking antimicrobial use, slaughterhouse contamination and human colonization. A coordinated One Health response should combine antimicrobial stewardship in livestock production, ante-mortem and post-mortem inspection, hygienic slaughter practices, worker protection, water and waste management, food-chain surveillance and genomic epidemiology. Strengthening these measures through regional collaboration could improve food safety and reduce opportunities for the dissemination of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in East Africa.
